content: The services described are specifically designed to facilitate the management of fecal sludge and/or wastewater through various stages, including containment, emptying, transport, treatment, and eventual end use or disposal. In this context, sanitation users refers to all individuals who utilize a toilet, while sanitation workers encompasses all individuals—whether formally employed or not—who are responsible for cleaning, maintaining, operating, or emptying sanitation technologies at any point along the sanitation chain. A separate (foul) sewer is a type of sewer system that transports blackwater and greywater but excludes stormwater. Sewage refers to wastewater that is conveyed through a sewer system. A sewer is an underground pipe system that carries blackwater, greywater, and, in some cases, stormwater (in combined sewer systems) from households and other users to treatment facilities, utilizing gravity or pumps as needed. A shared toilet is a single toilet facility used by two or more households. A soak pit is a pit or chamber designed to allow effluent to infiltrate into the surrounding soil. Stabilization is a treatment process that involves the biodegradation of easily degradable molecules in fecal sludge, resulting in a product with reduced oxygen demand. This process produces fecal sludge containing more stable, complex organic molecules that are less readily degradable. Stabilization is a key objective of treatment technologies. A standard refers to a required or agreed-upon level of quality or achievement. Stormwater is the term used for rainfall runoff collected from surfaces such as roofs and roads, which flows toward low-lying areas. It represents the portion of rainfall that does not infiltrate into the soil. The theory of change is a detailed explanation and illustration of how and why a desired change is expected to occur within a specific context. A toilet serves as the user interface with the sanitation system, capturing excreta. Toilets can include various designs, such as toilet seats, latrine slabs, pedestals, pans, or urinals, and may be of different types, including pour-flush, cistern-flush, dry toilets, or urine-diverting toilets. Treatment processes aim to alter the physical, chemical, and biological characteristics of fecal sludge or wastewater, converting it into a product that is safe for end use or disposal. Urine is the liquid waste produced by the body to eliminate urea and other waste products. In this context, urine product refers to pure urine that is not mixed with feces or water. Wastewater is used water originating from a combination of domestic (household and service), industrial, and stormwater sources, as well as any inflow or infiltration into sewer systems. The Guidelines on Sanitation and Health emphasize the critical role of safe sanitation in promoting health, from preventing infections to improving mental and social well-being. These guidelines were developed following the processes outlined in the WHO Handbook for Guideline Development and offer comprehensive advice on maximizing the health benefits of sanitation interventions. The guidelines summarize evidence on the links between sanitation and health, provide evidence-based recommendations, and offer guidance for international, national, and local sanitation policies and programs. The intended audience for these guidelines includes national and local authorities responsible for the safety of sanitation systems and services, such as policymakers, planners, and implementers within and outside the health sector, as well as those involved in the development, implementation, and monitoring of sanitation standards and regulations.
